hints: Focus on writing the actual chemical equation that each standard enthalpy term describes, starting from the named reactants.
Write out combustion of graphite as $\text{C(s) + O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$ and then write formation of $\text{CO}_2$ the same way.
Check whether the other pairs start from the same elements in the same states and make the same single product, or whether extra steps are involved.
walkthrough:
**Recall what each definition means**

Standard enthalpy changes are defined by a very specific reaction. Combustion means 1 mol of substance burns completely in oxygen. Formation means 1 mol of compound forms from its elements in standard states.

Rule to use:
$$\text{compare the balanced equations, not just the names}$$

**Test the graphite and carbon dioxide pair**

Combustion of graphite is burning 1 mol of carbon. Formation of $\text{CO}_2$ is making 1 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ from C and $\text{O}_2$.

Both reactions are:
$$\text{C(graphite) + O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$$

**Conclude the match**

Because the starting materials, the product, and the amounts are identical, the enthalpy change must be numerically identical. This is the only pair where the two definitions describe exactly the same chemical change.

options.A: Atomisation of $\text{CH}_4$ is $\text{CH}_4\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{C(g) + 4H(g)}$, which is strongly endothermic to break all C-H bonds. Formation of $\text{CH}_4$ is $\text{C(s) + 2H}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_4\text{(g)}$, which starts from different reactants and is exothermic. Different reactions, so values are not equal.
options.B: Combustion of $\text{CH}_3\text{OH(l)}$ is $\text{CH}_3\text{OH + 1.5O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The sum on the right is $\text{C + O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2$ plus $2(\text{H}_2 + 0.5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O})$. By Hess's Law they differ by the formation enthalpy of methanol, so they are not equal.
options.C: Both terms describe the identical reaction: $\text{C(graphite) + O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$. Burning 1 mol of graphite in excess oxygen gives 1 mol of $\text{CO}_2$, and forming 1 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ from its elements (C and $\text{O}_2$) is the same change. Hence $\Delta H_c$ of graphite equals $\Delta H_f$ of $\text{CO}_2$.
options.D: Neutralisation $\text{H}^+\text{(aq) + OH}^-\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ is about -57 kJ per mol of water from aqueous ions. Formation of $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ is $\text{H}_2\text{(g) + 0.5O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ from elements, about -286 kJ per mol. Different starting materials, so different values.
